title: MoSCoW prioritization
blurb: Use MoSCoW to prioritize requirements, and explain how fixing Must haves and flexing the rest protects time and cost.
question: Halfway through a release, the team realizes it cannot finish everything by the fixed date. Using MoSCoW, what should be flexed, and what must not be?

teach.body: MoSCoW is a quality practice technique for prioritizing requirements: Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time). The small o's just make the word sayable. PRINCE2 Agile uses it in backlog refinement and in defining scope, so that everyone agrees which requirements are essential and which can give way when time is short.

teach.h: Fix the Musts, flex the rest
teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile's default for scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves. Time and cost have zero tolerance on all levels of plan. So when the timebox is under pressure, the team does not extend the date or add budget: it gives up lower-priority Shoulds and Coulds, protecting the Musts. That is how MoSCoW keeps time and cost fixed.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 3.1, Table 5.1

head: Aspect
Default in PRINCE2 Agile
rows: Fixed: zero tolerance for extra time
Fixed: zero tolerance for extra cost
Flexed to protect time and cost
teach.caption: Agile allows tolerance on what is delivered and restricts tolerance on time and cost (Table 5.1).

children.edge: Coulds and Shoulds can absorb it
children.label: Drop or defer them

teach.body: In starting up, the scope definition topic of the project canvas workshop sets scope as epic user stories prioritized with MoSCoW and checks timeline and scope tolerances. In managing product delivery, the product backlog refinement topic of the team planning workshop reviews and prioritizes requirements using MoSCoW. The project brief also notes the flexible areas of scope and quality criteria that come from prioritization.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book Table 13.2, Table 13.13, Table 6.1

teach.body: Retailer Pellow and Finch must launch click-and-collect before its busiest month. Chief product owner Rhys Morgan marks 'reserve an item' and 'collect with a code' as Must haves, text alerts as a Should have, gift wrapping as a Could have, and same-day delivery as Won't have this time. When velocity drops, product owner Leanne Cho's team drops gift wrapping and keeps the date. Recording same-day delivery as Won't have stops it creeping back in.

teach.text: W means Won't have THIS TIME: agreed out for now, not rejected for ever. And the flex is in SCOPE (Shoulds and Coulds), not in time or cost. If even the Must haves cannot be delivered within tolerance, that is an exception for the board.

teach.body: MoSCoW comes from DSDM, which describes Must haves as the minimum usable subset, Should haves as important but not vital, Could haves as the main contingency and first to drop, and Won't haves as agreed out for this timeframe. DSDM advises that Must haves should not fill the whole timebox, so there is room to flex; treat its percentage guide (about 60% of effort) as background, not a PRINCE2 Agile rule.
teach.cite: DSDM handbook, MoSCoW (background, not a PRINCE2 Agile rule)

items: MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have (this time).
A quality practice technique used in backlog refinement and scope definition.
Scope fixed for Must haves; flexed for Should and Could haves (Table 3.1).
Time and cost: zero tolerance, so flex scope to protect them.
Used in the project canvas workshop (scope definition) and team planning workshop (backlog refinement).
If the Must haves cannot be delivered within tolerance, raise an exception.

summary: You can now name the four MoSCoW categories and explain that Must haves are fixed while Should and Could haves flex to protect zero-tolerance time and cost. You can also say where MoSCoW is used and what happens when even the Musts are at risk.

A.q: What does the W in MoSCoW stand for?
A.why: The four categories are Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time) (9.3.2).

whyNot.0: 'Would have' is not one of the MoSCoW categories.
whyNot.2: MoSCoW has no 'wish list' category; deferred items are Won't have this time.
whyNot.3: 'Wanted by the users' is not a category; all categories concern what users want.

A.q: In PRINCE2 Agile, how is scope treated by default?
options: Fixed for every requirement the board agreed at initiation
Flexed for Must haves first when the timebox is short
Fixed for Must haves; flexed for Should and Could haves
Flexed for all requirements to protect benefits
A.why: Table 3.1 fixes scope for Must haves and flexes it for Should and Could haves.

whyNot.0: Fixing all scope would remove the flexibility agile relies on to keep time and cost fixed.
whyNot.1: Must haves are the fixed part of scope; they are not flexed.
whyNot.3: Must haves are fixed, so not all requirements flex.

A.q: Which practice includes MoSCoW among its artifacts and techniques in PRINCE2 Agile?
A.why: MoSCoW is listed with the quality practice artifacts, used in backlog refinement and scope definition (9.3.2).

whyNot.1: The risk practice uses the Agilometer and the risk register.
whyNot.2: The progress practice uses dashboards, burn charts and the project log.
whyNot.3: The organization practice covers roles, team structure and the commercial approach.

B.q: A team forecasts it cannot complete every story in the release by the fixed date. What is the PRINCE2 Agile default response?
options: Extend the release date to deliver every story
Ask the board for extra budget to add developers
Move some Must haves into the next release
Drop or defer lower-priority Should and Could haves
B.why: Time and cost have zero tolerance, and scope flexes for Should and Could haves, so lower-priority items give way (Table 3.1).

whyNot.0: Time has zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so the date is not extended.
whyNot.1: Cost has zero tolerance, so adding budget is not the default response.
whyNot.2: Must haves are fixed scope; deferring them is not the default flex.

B.q: In which workshop topic is project scope set as epic user stories prioritized with MoSCoW?
options: Scope definition in the project canvas workshop
Iteration planning in the team planning workshop
Release planning in the release planning workshop
Risk analysis in the starting up workshop
B.why: The scope definition topic of the project canvas workshop sets scope in epic user stories prioritized with MoSCoW and checks timeline and scope tolerances (Table 13.2).

whyNot.1: Iteration planning selects stories for the next iteration based on priority and estimates.
whyNot.2: Release planning breaks key activities into stories and updates the release map.
whyNot.3: Risk analysis identifies threats and opportunities for initiation and the project.

B.q:
Which two statements about MoSCoW in PRINCE2 Agile are correct?
1. Should and Could haves can be flexed to protect time and cost.
2. Won't have this time means the item is rejected for good.
3. MoSCoW is used when refining the product backlog.
4. Must haves are the first items to drop when time is short.
B.why: Shoulds and Coulds flex to protect fixed time and cost (1), and MoSCoW is used in product backlog refinement (3) (Table 3.1, Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: Won't have this time is out for this timeframe, not rejected for good.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: Won't haves are deferred not rejected, and Must haves are the fixed part of scope.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is wrong: Must haves are fixed; lower-priority items drop first.

C.q: Technical problems mean that the remaining Must haves can no longer be delivered within the stage tolerances. What does this cause, and which report should the project manager produce?
options: A detail change; an issue report
A lesson; an end stage report
C.why: Must haves are fixed scope, so a forecast that they cannot be delivered within tolerance is an exception, reported to the board in an exception report (Table 3.1, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: Failing to deliver fixed Must haves is beyond tolerance, not a detail change inside the backlog.
whyNot.2: The problem has happened and is forecast to breach tolerance; a highlight report is routine status.
whyNot.3: This needs a board decision now, not just a lesson or an end stage report.

C.q: In the team planning workshop, which topic uses MoSCoW, and what is it trying to achieve?
options: Effort estimation; a shared view of story size
User story refinement; testable acceptance criteria
Iteration planning; a realistic team plan
C.why: Product backlog refinement reviews and prioritizes requirements using MoSCoW, so the team understands the stories and agrees priorities (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Effort estimation builds a shared view of complexity and effort, not MoSCoW priorities.
whyNot.1: User story refinement makes acceptance criteria clear and testable.
whyNot.3: Iteration planning selects stories into the team plan using existing priorities and estimates.

C.q: Which performance aspects are protected by flexing Should and Could haves, and what tolerance do they have by default?
options: Benefits and risk; tolerance set by the CPO
Scope and quality; tolerance set by the team
Time and cost; zero tolerance on all plans
Sustainability and scope; tolerance above minimum
C.why: Time and cost have zero tolerance on all levels of plan, so lower-priority scope flexes to protect them (Table 3.1, Table 5.1).

whyNot.0: Benefits are fixed at minimum viability and flexed above it; the CPO does not set tolerances.
whyNot.1: Scope is the aspect that flexes, not the one being protected, and teams do not set tolerances.
whyNot.3: Sustainability is fixed for minimum criteria; scope is the aspect being flexed.

reteach.title: Packing for a fixed-weight flight
reteach.question: Why does MoSCoW make it possible to keep the date and the budget fixed?

blocks.body: Your airline allows one 20 kg bag: the weight limit is like fixed time and cost. Passport and tickets are Must haves. A warm coat is a Should have: you would miss it, but you could buy one there. A second pair of trainers is a Could have, first out if the bag is heavy. The surfboard is a Won't have this time. You pack to the limit by leaving lower priorities out.

blocks.text: Never answer 'extend the date' or 'add budget' to a scope squeeze in PRINCE2 Agile. Flex Shoulds and Coulds; if the Musts are at risk, it is an exception.

explain.body: Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time. The o's are only there to make the word pronounceable.

test.q: Which list gives the MoSCoW categories in order?
options: Must, Should, Could, Won't this time
test.why: MoSCoW stands for Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have (this time) (9.3.2).

whyNot.1: Can and Will later are not MoSCoW categories.
whyNot.2: These labels are not the MoSCoW categories.
whyNot.3: Mandatory and Wish are not the MoSCoW category names.

explain.body: Scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves. Time and cost have zero tolerance.

test.q: Which requirements are fixed by default in PRINCE2 Agile?
test.why: Scope is fixed for Must haves (Table 3.1).

whyNot.2: Won't haves are not being delivered this time, so there is nothing to fix.

explain.body: Scope definition in the project canvas workshop prioritizes epics with MoSCoW; product backlog refinement in the team planning workshop prioritizes stories with it.

test.q: In which workshop does a team prioritize its product backlog using MoSCoW before each iteration?
test.why: The product backlog refinement topic of the team planning workshop prioritizes requirements using MoSCoW (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: The progress review workshop reviews status, risks and the product demo.
whyNot.2: The kickoff workshop builds the team, values and dashboards.
whyNot.3: The retrospective reflects on the last iteration: the good, the bad, the learning, team building.

explain.h: When even Musts are at risk
explain.body: Flexing Shoulds and Coulds handles normal pressure. If the Must haves are forecast not to be delivered within tolerance, the project manager raises an exception with the board.

test.q: What does a forecast that some Must haves cannot be delivered within tolerance lead to?
test.why: Must haves are fixed scope, so failing to deliver them within tolerance is an exception, raised to the board in an exception report (Table 3.1, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: Trading swaps items of similar effort; it cannot make undeliverable Musts deliverable within tolerance.
whyNot.1: A retrospective reflects on the iteration; it does not handle a tolerance breach.
whyNot.3: The DoR controls when work may start; it does not resolve a breach of scope tolerance.
